children.text: The Basilica Minore of Our Lady of Peñafrancia, in Barangay Balatas in Naga City, is the only basilica in the Bicol region and a national shrine. Dedicated in 1982 and raised to basilica status in 1985, it is the destination of the September festival and draws pilgrims in large numbers.
Officially named the Minor Basilica and National Shrine of Our Lady of Peñafrancia, this Catholic church belongs to the Archdiocese of Cáceres and is
the only basilica in the entire Bicol region

. It stands on a three-hectare lot in the Balatas district, a short distance from downtown Naga. Do not confuse it with the Naga Metropolitan Cathedral in the same city or the old shrine across the river, which are different buildings, so check the name carefully on your map.

The story begins in 1960, when Archbishop Pedro Paulo Santos planned a large church able to hold the pilgrims, since the old shrine could not take the crowds that arrive every September feast. Work started with a groundbreaking on
April 18, 1976

, was delayed by funding problems, was completed in September 1981, and the church was blessed and dedicated on May 22, 1982. On May 22, 1985, Pope John Paul II conferred the title of Minor Basilica, and it later also came to be called a national shrine.

The building is a modern cruciform church with white and canary-yellow walls and a green roof, built around a repeating arch motif. A large arched window of stained glass fills the facade, and small domes crown the crossing and the bell tower. According to Wikipedia, it has seating for about 1,500 and room for about 2,700 including standing worshippers. Inside, the high ceiling and clerestory windows make the nave airy and bright.

The heart of the church is the image of Ina (Mother) Mary, said to have been commissioned in 1710 by Fr. Miguel de Covarrubias. Normally the image is enshrined in the basilica; during the annual September festival it is carried to the cathedral and then returns by a fluvial procession. This makes the basilica a quiet place of prayer on ordinary days and the stage where devotees from all over Bicol gather during festival week. For travelers who want to explore religious heritage at a relaxed pace, it is the core of any Naga itinerary.
Raised to basilica status in 1985, it is the only one in the Bicol region and in the whole Archdiocese of Cáceres. Pilgrims often say this alone is
a reason to come to Naga
. It also holds the status of national shrine.

blocks.title: Ina and the Prayer with the Mantle

children.text: The image of Ina is enshrined here. After the 4:00 PM Saturday Mass, a healing prayer using Mary's mantle (manto) and a Marian procession are said to follow. Schedules can change, so confirm before you go.

The large arched facade window and the clerestory windows are all stained glass. They are described as showing the history of Marian devotion in Bicol and scenes of the Naga River fluvial procession. The interior colors are best when morning sunlight comes through.

Arches repeat across the facade, crossing, windows, doorways and bell tower, forming the church's design motif. The combination of white walls, yellow accents and a green roof stands out from a distance. The forecourt and lawn in front of the church are popular photo spots.

blocks.title: The End of the Festival Route

children.text: In the September Peñafrancia Festival, the basilica is the destination of the Naga River fluvial procession. In 2026 the schedule was the fluvial procession on September 19 and the feast day Mass on September 20. Large Masses are held after the image returns, so festival week feels completely different from a normal day.

Visit reports mention a pavilion that shelters the image of Mary after large processions. It features a small dome, a glass roof and stained glass panels. Whether it is open depends on the time of year, so check on site.

The Naga City tourism site notes a shop within walking distance that sells crucifixes, holy cards, statuettes and replicas of Ina's mantle. A Peñafrancia Basilica Museum is also marked on maps. Opening hours are irregular, so leave some flexibility in your schedule.

items.title: Half-Day Pilgrimage Route
items.subtitle: From the city cathedral to the basilica

children.text: Start at Naga Metropolitan Cathedral and Porta Mariae to get a sense of the city's religious heritage. A seminary and museums are also clustered around the cathedral.
Take a jeepney or tricycle to Balatas. Visitors report the jeepney ride from downtown takes about
20 minutes
Admire the exterior, the bell tower and the stained glass facade from the forecourt, then step inside and sit quietly.
This is the time slot announced for the weekday
English Mass. If your schedule allows, attend the Mass or observe quietly from the back.
Look around the souvenir shop in front of the church, then head back downtown for lunch.

Mass times vary by day and season. Check the basilica's official Facebook page or call for the latest schedule before you go. If you arrive early in the morning, the interior is quietest and sunlight passing through the stained glass makes for good photos. If you plan to stay longer than half a day, continue to the museums and market in downtown Naga in the afternoon.

items.title: September Festival Week Route
items.subtitle: A day at the end of the fluvial procession

children.text: Soak up the novena atmosphere around the cathedral and along the Naga River. During the festival, downtown roads are closed.
On the day of the fluvial procession, claim a riverside viewing spot early. One guide recommends securing a spot near the Panganiban Bridge by around
This is the time the image returns to the basilica. The crowds are very large, so follow the instructions of marshals.
The feast day Mass is held at the basilica. Arrive early to find a seat; many people follow the Mass outdoors on large screens.
Festival dates and procession times change every year. Always check the Naga City tourism announcement for that year.
Long-distance buses to Naga leave from PITX, Cubao, Alabang and other terminals. The trip takes about
10 hours
Regular seats are said to cost about

. Fares differ by operator and season.
During the September festival, book 3–4 weeks ahead, or 6–8 weeks ahead for sleeper seats.
In Naga, you can reach Balatas by city jeepney or tricycle.
Cebgo operates one daily flight from NAIA to Naga Airport (WNP), taking about
1 hour
One-way fares are quoted at about
and vary widely by season. Check the latest fare.
Naga Airport is said to be about
10 km

items.title: From Downtown Naga to the Basilica

children.text: Take a jeepney bound for Balatas from downtown, get off at Balatas and walk. The fare is about
Tricycles are said to cost about
from downtown, but you will need to negotiate. Before boarding, confirm whether it is a regular or a special fare.
Grab is convenient with luggage or at night.
The basilica is about
20 minutes
from downtown. From the airport, it is usual to go into the city first and transfer. On map apps, search for Basilica Loop, Balatas to get the exact location.

The basilica is open year-round and is quietest on weekday mornings. In the dry season it is easier to move around the forecourt and nearby areas, while in the rainy season you spend more time inside the church out of the rain.

September has a completely different atmosphere because of the Peñafrancia Festival. If you want the religious experience, September is worth a visit, but you should arrange lodging and transport months ahead.

Masses are announced on weekdays in Bikol and English at around 6 and 7 in the morning, 11 at midday and 5 in the evening, with more Masses on Sundays. Exact times can change week to week, so check official channels before you go. The Holy Rosary is said on weekdays at 6:45 AM and 4:45 PM, with the novena to Our Mother of Perpetual Help on Wednesdays, the novena to the Divino Rostro on Fridays and the novena to Our Lady of Peñafrancia on Saturdays.

It is more convenient to stay in downtown Naga than right in front of the basilica. Downtown has restaurants and transport close by, so it is easy to make a jeepney trip to the basilica. Ordinary guesthouses run about
, and prices rise sharply during the September festival, so book 2–3 months ahead.
Be sure to try Bicol regional cooking. Bicol Express, made with coconut milk and chilies, and laing are typical. Street food is said to cost
a dish and a sit-down meal
per person.

After visiting the basilica, the easiest plan is to return downtown for a meal. There are simple stalls for pilgrims around the church but not much choice, so it helps to bring snacks and water from downtown in the morning. Visitors from abroad are encouraged to taste Bicol regional dishes and Filipino snacks at Naga's markets and restaurant areas.
Dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered. Taking off hats and sunglasses inside the church is a courtesy.
Keep quiet during Mass and do not eat or drink inside the church. Photography is generally allowed, but do not use flash during Mass.
It is relatively quiet at the 6–8 AM weekday Masses and after the 4:00 PM Mass. On Sundays there are several Masses and many worshippers.
Mass and prayer schedules change often. Check the latest schedule through the official email, Facebook page, or by phone at (054) 473 3644.
When riding a jeepney from downtown, say you are going to Balatas and confirm exactly where to get off. Agree on the fare before boarding a tricycle.
During the September festival, roads are closed and mobile signal may be poor, so decide on a meeting point with your group beforehand.
Combined with Naga's downtown sights, one day is enough. It pairs well with the cathedral, the old shrine and the university museum.
This is a national shrine and a place of pilgrimage, so when taking photos take care not to frame the faces of people at prayer. Wait your turn in line near the image.
During the festival there are road closures and extreme crowding, so take special care of valuables and your group.
Mass times and prayer schedules change by season, so check official channels for the latest information before you visit.
This is a religious site, so do not speak loudly or touch the image disrespectfully during events.
Pickpockets increase in crowds. Carry your bag in front and keep it zipped.
Tricycles add special fares during the festival. Agree on a fixed fare before you ride.
Do not push into the traditional area of the voyadores (male volunteers) in the image's procession as a foreigner.
The city's cathedral is about
20 minutes
away by jeepney. It is also where the September novenas are held.
Bicol's biggest religious festival, whose fluvial procession ends at the basilica.
The central city of Bicol, with restaurants, museums and markets.
The old shrine across the Naga River is where the Traslacion begins. It is a different building from the basilica, so you can visit both.
